content.text: Flutter's official architecture guide strongly recommends a UI layer and a data layer, built from views, view models, repositories and services. The domain layer, where use cases live, is marked optional and "Conditional". Add a use case when logic merges repositories, gets complex or is reused, and let simple view models call repositories directly.
A three-person team adds a dark mode switch to its Flutter app. The pull request touches nine files: an abstract repository and its implementation, a local data source,
GetThemeModeUseCase
and
SetThemeModeUseCase

, an entity, a model, a mapper and a view model. A reviewer asks why a switch needs nine files. The author answers that this is clean Flutter architecture, the way the official guide says to do it. Then the reviewer opens the guide and finds the domain layer under a heading that starts with "Optional".
The common misconception
The belief: good Flutter architecture means three layers, presentation, domain and data, for every feature, and every action the UI takes goes through its own use-case class, no matter how simple.

It's a reasonable belief. Clean Architecture templates for Flutter look exactly like this, and starter kits generate the folders for you. A fixed shape feels safe: every feature looks the same, and nobody argues about where code goes. Use cases are easy to unit test. And the official guide does describe a domain layer, with use cases, and its sample app has a few. The half-truth: use cases are a real tool that the guide recommends, but only under conditions it spells out.
What actually happens
The guide's core is two layers, not three

The guide calls separation of concerns "the most important principle" and says your app "should split into two broad layers, the UI layer and the Data layer." It recommends four components: views, view models, repositories and services. In
MVVM
terms, views and view models are the UI layer, and repositories and services are the model.

Its description of a feature is just as specific: one view, one view model, "one or more repositories as the sources of truth for your application data, and zero or more services". No use case appears in that list. The domain layer shows up first in a note: "Apps with complex logic might also have a logic layer".
"Conditional" is the official rating

The recommendations page rates every practice: "Strongly recommend", "Recommend" or "Conditional". Clearly defined UI and data layers, the repository pattern, MVVM and abstract repository classes are all strongly recommended. "Use a domain layer" is conditional, with a blunt explanation: "In very large apps, use-cases are useful, but in most apps they add unnecessary overhead."
The guide gives three conditions for moving logic out of a view model into a
use case

. The logic merges data from several repositories, it's "exceedingly complex", or it's reused by different view models. If none applies, the guide's answer is direct: "This layer is optional because not all applications or features within an application have these requirements."
Add them when needed, not up front

The guide also asks whether view models may still read repositories directly, or must always go through use cases. If you force a use case "each time a view model needs data, even if the logic in the use-case is simple", your code will be modular and testable, "but it also adds a significant amount of unnecessary overhead." Its advice: "add use-cases only when needed." The guide's own example app practices this: it has use cases for some features and view models that talk to repositories directly.

Android's architecture guidance, which Flutter's closely resembles, says the same: the domain layer is "optional", and "A good approach is to add use cases only when required." It also warns that its "domain layer" differs from the one in Clean Architecture, so the two vocabularies shouldn't be mixed up. A pass-through use case is a small case of
YAGNI
: an abstraction built for a need that hasn't arrived.
Cutting the pass-through, keeping the real one

content.text: The settings view model is just as testable without the use case: give it a fake
SettingsRepository
, which the guide recommends anyway.
BookTripUseCase
is different. It coordinates two repositories, and both the booking screen and a "book again" button need it, so it meets two of the guide's three conditions. Using Bloc or Riverpod instead of
ChangeNotifier
doesn't change the reasoning; the case study says the same app could have been written with them.

A domain layer with use cases
Separate API models and domain models

blocks.title: Optional use cases don't mean optional structure

content.text: The opposite mistake is worse: dropping the view model and putting logic in widgets. "Do not put logic in widgets" is strongly recommended, and the guide limits views to simple show-and-hide conditions, animation, layout and simple routing. A use case you skip moves into the view model, never into
build()

blocks.title: Let the second caller create the use case

content.text: Write the logic in the view model first. When a second view model needs the same logic, or the first one starts combining repositories, extract a use case named after its action, like Android's
FormatDateUseCase
. Refactoring a method into a class later is cheap; deleting forty pass-through classes is not.
The same idea runs through ReadIn's articles on coupling and cohesion and on Clean Architecture as a dependency rule: layers and classes are tools for managing change, not a score to maximize.
How to apply it in your project
For each one, ask: does it merge repositories, hold complex logic, or serve more than one view model? If the answer is no to all three, inline it into the view model.
Views without logic, view models per feature, repositories as the source of truth, services per data source, and abstract repositories with fakes for tests.
Let view models call repositories unless a use case adds something. Both guides suggest restricting access only if nearly all data already flows through use cases.
When duplication or cross-repository logic appears, create the use case then, and name it after its action.
Put "use cases when needed" in your architecture notes, so reviews stop asking for a use case per feature.
Key takeaways

items.text: Flutter's guide strongly recommends two layers: UI (views, view models) and data (repositories, services).
The domain layer is officially "Conditional"; the guide says that in most apps use cases "add unnecessary overhead".
Add a use case when logic merges repositories, is very complex, or is reused by several view models.
View models may call repositories directly; a pass-through use case adds files, not value.
Skipping use cases never means putting logic in widgets.
